RW_M1.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “yields” most nearly mean?
RW_M1.passage: Netting is used in engineering wherever a surface must catch something without stopping the air. A net stretched below a bridge deck slows a falling worker over a long distance instead of over the inch or two a solid platform would allow. Its mesh <u>yields</u> as the load comes on, and the force never rises to the value a rigid surface would produce.
RW_M1.why: The mesh is described as slowing a fall over a long distance, so it stretches under the load. The 'produces' sense of the word is the one used of a crop or a return, which does not fit a mesh under a falling weight.

RW_M1.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
RW_M1.passage: Charcoal drawn on a cave wall can be dated directly, because the carbon in it once belonged to a living tree. A figure drawn in red ochre cannot: the pigment is a mineral, and its age is the age of the rock, not of the hand that ground it. The two techniques of the same cave are therefore not equally _____.
RW_M1.why: The passage contrasts charcoal, which can be dated, with ochre, which cannot, so the blank is about yielding a date. The 'durable' option concerns survival, and the text says nothing about either pigment fading.

RW_M1.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
RW_M1.passage: Basaltic lava is runny enough to spread in sheets and to travel miles from its vent, while the stiffer lava of some other volcanoes piles up over the opening it came from. The shape of a volcano is thus largely _____ by the chemistry of what it erupts.
RW_M1.why: Two chemistries are shown producing two shapes, so the chemistry fixes the form. The 'obscured' option would mean the chemistry hides the shape rather than setting it.

RW_M1.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
RW_M1.passage: Sailcloth is graded by the weight of a fixed area of it, and a loft keeps several grades on hand. A cloth heavy enough to hold its shape in a gale is needlessly stiff in light air, while a light cloth that draws well in a breeze will stretch out of shape when pressed. Choosing a grade is thus an exercise in _____ rather than in finding a single best cloth.
RW_M1.why: Each grade is described as good in one condition and bad in the other, so the choice trades one advantage against another. The 'improvisation' option suggests working without a plan, but the text describes a deliberate selection from known grades.

RW_M1.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
RW_M1.passage: Louis Braille's cells use at most six dots, few enough that a fingertip takes in a whole character at rest. Earlier raised alphabets copied the shapes of printed letters, which the finger had to trace curve by curve. Braille's design succeeded because it was _____ to the sense that would read it rather than to the eye.
RW_M1.why: The contrast is between a system matched to how a fingertip works and one copied from print, so the blank names a fit with touch. The 'indifferent' option would say the design took no account of touch, which is the reverse of the point.

RW_M1.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
RW_M1.passage: Two figures on the same cave wall need not be the same age. A wall may be painted, left for a thousand years and painted again, and nothing in the images announces the gap. Dating a cave therefore means dating each mark that can be dated and admitting that the rest float free, rather than assigning a single date to the chamber and its contents together.
RW_M1.why: The passage argues from the possibility of long gaps between paintings to the practice of dating each datable mark separately. Saying that most paintings were made close together is the assumption the text is written against.

choices.label: A
choices.content: A cave's paintings must be dated individually, because a single date for the whole wall cannot be justified.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Most cave paintings were made within a short period of one another.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Radiocarbon dating is the only method available for cave art.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Caves were repainted so often that their earliest images are lost.

RW_M1.stem: What is the main purpose of the text?
RW_M1.passage: A sail is not a flat sheet. The sailmaker cuts each cloth with a slight curve along the edge that will be sewn to its neighbour, so that when the panels are joined the finished sail bellies out into a shape it will hold under wind. The curve is measured in inches over the length of a seam, and a loft floor is marked out full size so that it can be laid off exactly.
RW_M1.why: The passage moves from the claim that a sail is not flat to the seam curves and the full-size floor markings that create the shape, which is a description of a method. Nothing in the text compares hand work with machine work.

choices.label: A
choices.content: To explain how a curved sail is produced from flat pieces of cloth.

choices.label: B
choices.content: To argue that hand cutting produces better sails than machine cutting.

choices.label: C
choices.content: To trace the history of the sailmaking loft as a building.

choices.label: D
choices.content: To compare the shapes of sails used in different kinds of weather.

RW_M1.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
RW_M1.passage: A wire rope is stronger than a steel bar of the same weight, but that is not why it is used on a crane. A bar of the necessary section could not be wound round a drum: bending it once would leave a permanent set, and bending it repeatedly would crack it. A rope made of many thin wires bends because each wire moves a little against its neighbours, and it can be wound and unwound thousands of times.
RW_M1.why: The passage sets aside strength in its first sentence and spends the rest on the bending that a bar cannot survive and a rope can. Comparing strength at the same dimensions misstates the opening, which compares them at the same weight.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Thin wires are easier to manufacture than bars of large section.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Wire rope is used on cranes chiefly because it can be bent repeatedly without damage.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Wire rope is stronger than any solid steel bar of the same dimensions.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Crane drums are designed to reduce the bending a rope must undergo.

RW_M1.stem: According to the text, what makes it possible to re-cover a sewn book without disturbing the leaves?
RW_M1.passage: A sewn book is built from folded gatherings, and the sewing thread passes through the fold of each one and round a cord laid across the spine. Because the cords are then laced into the boards, the covers are attached to the sewing rather than to the paper. A binding of this kind can be pulled off its boards and re-covered without the leaves being disturbed.
RW_M1.why: The passage says the cords are laced into the boards and that the covers are therefore attached to the sewing rather than to the paper. Glue along the spine is the opposite of the structure described, in which the thread runs through the folds.

choices.label: A
choices.content: The leaves are trimmed after the covers have been fitted.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The thread passes round the outside of each gathering rather than through it.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The covers are held by cords attached to the sewing rather than to the paper itself.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The gatherings are glued to one another along the spine.

RW_M1.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Vollan's argument?
RW_M1.passage:
A rope's residual strength was measured after it had been bent repeatedly round sheaves of different diameters, expressed as a multiple of the rope's own diameter. Rigging researcher Marte Vollan argues that sheave diameter matters far more to the life of a rope than the number of bends it undergoes.
Sheave diameterStrength retained after 10,000 bendsStrength retained after 40,000 bends
10 times rope diameter58%51%
20 times rope diameter89%85%
30 times rope diameter96%94%
RW_M1.why: Setting the loss from four times as many bends beside the loss from changing sheave size is the only comparison that ranks the two factors, which is what the argument asserts. Quoting the smallest sheave's two figures describes one row and never brings the sheave sizes into comparison with one another.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Ropes bent round the largest sheave retained 96 percent of their strength after 10,000 bends.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Every rope in the trial lost some strength as the number of bends increased.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Quadrupling the number of bends cost each rope at most 7 percentage points of strength, while going from the largest sheave to the smallest cost 38 points at 10,000 bends.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Ropes bent round the smallest sheave retained 58 percent of their strength after 10,000 bends and 51 percent after 40,000.

RW_M1.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Halloran's argument?
RW_M1.passage: The panels of a sail are cut so that the threads of the cloth run along the line of greatest pull. Sail designer Petra Halloran argues that a sail's tendency to lose its shape after a season depends more on how the panels were laid out than on the grade of cloth used.
RW_M1.why: Holding the cloth constant while varying the layout, and then the reverse, isolates layout as the thing that governs the change in shape. That heavier cloth stretches less under a fixed load is a property of the cloth and leaves the comparison with layout untouched.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Sails cut in two different panel layouts from the same bolt of cloth differed markedly in how much their shape had changed after a season, while sails of different cloth grades cut in the same layout differed hardly at all.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Heavier cloth grades were found to stretch less than lighter grades under a fixed load.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Sails cut in the more common layout were quicker to make than sails cut in the other.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Sailmakers disagree about which of the two layouts should be used for a given sail.

RW_M1.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Oyelaran's argument?
RW_M1.passage:
Readers of contracted braille and readers of the uncontracted form were timed on the same passages and then tested on what they had understood. Reading specialist Denise Oyelaran argues that the contracted form's advantage is one of speed alone.
GroupWords per minuteComprehension score
Contracted braille11882%
Uncontracted braille7481%
RW_M1.why: Speed alone as the advantage requires the reading rates to differ while the comprehension scores do not, and only the pairing of both figures shows that. The reading rates on their own establish the advantage but say nothing about whether it is the only one.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Contracted readers read at 118 words per minute, while uncontracted readers read at 74.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Contracted readers scored 82 percent on comprehension, and uncontracted readers scored 81 percent.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Both groups read the same passages before being tested on what they had understood.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Contracted readers read at 118 words per minute against 74, but scored 82 percent on comprehension against 81 percent.

RW_M1.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
RW_M1.passage: Sailcloth woven from a fibre that creeps under sustained load will slowly lengthen while it is held taut, and a sail that has lengthened no longer presents the curve it was cut to. Laminated cloths hold their length because the load is carried by straight fibres bonded between films rather than by a woven structure that can pull tighter. A sail made from such a laminate should therefore _____
RW_M1.why: Creep is tied to loss of the designed curve, and the laminate is said not to creep, so its shape should last longer. Weight is never compared, and the passage gives no basis for ranking the two cloths by it.

choices.label: A
choices.content: prove easier to repair than a woven sail.

choices.label: B
choices.content: stretch further before it reaches its breaking load.

choices.label: C
choices.content: hold its designed shape for longer than a woven sail of similar weight.

choices.label: D
choices.content: be lighter than a woven sail of the same area.

RW_M1.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
RW_M1.passage: Translation systems trained on parallel text reproduce the distribution of the text they were trained on. A corpus assembled from parliamentary proceedings is heavy with formal argument and light on the language of a kitchen or a playground. A system trained on such a corpus alone can be expected to _____
RW_M1.why: If the system reproduces the distribution of its training text, and that text is rich in formal argument and poor in everyday speech, its performance should follow the same shape. Steady improvement through use is not something the passage attributes to these systems.

choices.label: A
choices.content: translate between any two languages with equal facility.

choices.label: B
choices.content: produce shorter sentences than the ones it was trained on.

choices.label: C
choices.content: improve steadily as it is used, without further training.

choices.label: D
choices.content: handle formal argument better than everyday conversation.

RW_M1.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
RW_M1.passage: The ropewalk at Chatham is a quarter of a mile long and still in use. The building's single purpose is written into its _____ else needs a room that shape.
RW_M1.why: A colon can stand between a complete statement and the explanation that follows it, which is the relation here. Setting the two off with only a comma joins two complete sentences with no conjunction.

RW_M1.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
RW_M1.passage: The load a fibre bundle can carry depends on how the load is shared out among its _____ and the sharing depends in turn on how tightly the bundle is twisted.
RW_M1.why: Two complete statements joined by the conjunction take a comma before it. A semicolon in front of a conjunction joining two main clauses is not a standard construction.

RW_M1.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
RW_M1.passage: The fungal threads that sheathe a root are thinner than the finest root _____ they reach into pores no root could enter.
RW_M1.why: A comma precedes the coordinating conjunction that joins two complete statements. Omitting the comma runs them together.

RW_M1.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
RW_M1.passage: When a flow's crust thickens enough to bear a person's _____ the lava beneath it may still be moving at walking pace.
RW_M1.why: The sentence opens with a subordinate clause, which is followed by a comma before the main clause. A semicolon cannot follow a clause that is not itself complete.

RW_M1.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
RW_M1.passage: The system had been trained on parliamentary proceedings, so its rendering of kitchen talk _____ nobody by being stilted.
RW_M1.why: The main clause needs a finite verb in a tense consistent with the past perfect that opens the sentence. The bare and participial forms leave the clause without a main verb.

RW_M1.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
RW_M1.passage: The binder laced the cords into the boards and then _____ the whole in calf.
RW_M1.why: The two verbs joined by the conjunction describe one sequence of actions and must share a tense, and the first is in the past. The present forms break that agreement.

RW_M1.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
RW_M1.passage: Witnesses who were told that they had picked the suspect later reported that _____ view of the face had been clearer than it was.
RW_M1.why: The blank calls for the possessive pronoun that belongs with the plural subject. The other spellings are an adverb, a contraction of a pronoun and a verb, and a singular possessive.

RW_M1.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
RW_M1.passage: Lava moving inside a tube is shielded from the air and loses heat slowly. _____ the tube confines the flow to a narrow path instead of letting it spread out and thin.
RW_M1.why: The second sentence names a further effect of the tube alongside the one already given, so an additive transition is called for. A contrastive marker would set the narrow path against the slow heat loss, and the two work together.

RW_M1.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
RW_M1.passage: Sailcloth is graded by weight, and a heavier grade holds its shape better under load. _____ a sail cut from the heaviest grade available will not set well in light air.
RW_M1.why: The second sentence limits what the first appears to recommend, so a contrastive transition is needed. A consequence marker would suggest the poor performance follows from the advantage just described.

RW_M1.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
RW_M1.passage: Wire rope is used wherever a load must be lifted round a drum or a sheave rather than hauled in a straight line. _____ a crane's hoisting gear runs its rope over three sheaves and on to a drum, bending it four times in every lift.
RW_M1.why: The second sentence gives a particular case of the general practice stated in the first, so the transition must introduce an illustration. A consequence marker would make the crane's arrangement follow from the general statement rather than exemplify it.

RW_M1.stem: The student wants to explain the limits of invariants to an audience unfamiliar with knot theory. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
RW_M1.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • A knot invariant assigns a value to a knot diagram.
  • Deforming the diagram without cutting leaves the value unchanged.
  • Two diagrams with different values must be different knots.
  • Two diagrams with the same value may still be different knots.
  • No invariant known distinguishes every pair of distinct knots.
RW_M1.why: The limit is the asymmetry between what differing and matching values prove, together with the gap no invariant closes, and only one sentence states both. Explaining that deformation leaves the value unchanged describes how invariants work rather than where they fall short.

choices.label: A
choices.content: A knot invariant assigns a value to a diagram, and deforming the diagram leaves that value unchanged.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Two diagrams with different values must be different knots, and deformation never changes a value.

choices.label: C
choices.content: No invariant known distinguishes every pair of distinct knots, though each assigns a value to a diagram.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Differing values prove that two diagrams are different knots, but matching values prove nothing, and no known invariant separates every pair.

RW_M1.stem: The student wants to emphasise that the stronger join is not always the one a rigger wants. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
RW_M1.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • A knot costs a rope about a third of its strength where it bends round itself.
  • A splice tucks the strands of one rope in among another's.
  • A spliced join keeps most of the rope's strength.
  • A splice takes far longer to make than a knot.
  • A splice cannot be cast off in a hurry.
RW_M1.why: The point is that strength alone does not settle the choice, so the sentence has to set the spliced join's advantage against the time it costs to undo. Describing the splice's hold on the rope's strength alone names the stronger join and drops the reason a knot is ever preferred.

choices.label: A
choices.content: A splice keeps most of a rope's strength where a knot costs about a third of it, but a splice cannot be cast off in a hurry, so a join that may have to be let go quickly is knotted instead.

choices.label: B
choices.content: A knot costs a rope about a third of its strength where it bends round itself, and a splice takes far longer to make.

choices.label: C
choices.content: A splice tucks the strands of one rope in among another's and keeps most of the rope's strength.

choices.label: D
choices.content: A splice takes far longer to make than a knot does and cannot be cast off in a hurry.

RW_M1.stem: The student wants to explain to an audience unfamiliar with the trade why the Chatham ropewalk is so long. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
RW_M1.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • A ropewalk is a long narrow building in which rope is laid.
  • The Chatham ropewalk, built in 1729, is 346 metres long.
  • Its length was set by the length of the cables made in it.
  • Cables for a first-rate warship were about 200 metres long.
  • The building is still used to make rope today.
RW_M1.why: The goal is to account for the length, and only the sentence pairing the building's dimension with the full-length laying of cables of about 200 metres supplies the reason. Noting that the building is still in use is true but says nothing about why it is long.

choices.label: A
choices.content: The Chatham ropewalk, built in 1729, is 346 metres long because rope was laid at full length, and the cables made there ran to about 200 metres.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The Chatham ropewalk, built in 1729, is 346 metres long and is still used to make rope today.

choices.label: C
choices.content: A ropewalk is a long narrow building, and the one at Chatham was built in 1729.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Cables for a first-rate warship were about 200 metres long, and the Chatham ropewalk is still in use.

RW_M2E.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
RW_M2E.passage: To a mathematician a knot is a closed loop in space, and two knots count as the same if one can be slid and stretched into the other without cutting the strand. Because such a deformation can leave a diagram looking utterly unlike the one it started from, telling two knots apart by eye is _____.
RW_M2E.why: If sliding and stretching can make the same knot look completely different, appearance is a poor guide to identity. The 'inexpensive' option speaks to cost, which the sentence never raises.

RW_M2E.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
RW_M2E.passage: A book sewn through the folds of its gathered sheets opens flat, because every leaf is held by thread that runs along the fold rather than by glue applied to a cut edge. Modern paperback bindings, which saw off the folds and glue the raw edges, gain speed of manufacture but _____ that behaviour.
RW_M2E.why: The sentence sets a gain in speed against something lost, and the flat opening belongs to the sewn structure that the glued binding cuts away. The 'recover' option would mean the glued binding restores the very property the sawing destroys.

RW_M2E.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
RW_M2E.passage: Asked to describe a face they had seen once, witnesses in one study grew markedly more confident after being told that another witness had picked the same person. Their accounts did not become more accurate. Confidence and accuracy, the researchers concluded, can move _____.
RW_M2E.why: Confidence rose while accuracy did not, so the two are shown to vary without reference to each other. The 'simultaneously' option would mean they rose together, which is the opposite of what the study found.

RW_M2E.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
RW_M2E.passage: A bacterium that carries a gene for resistance pays for it: making the protein costs energy that would otherwise go to growth. Where the drug is absent, such bacteria are outbred by their unburdened neighbours. Resistance is therefore not simply acquired and kept but _____ by the presence of the drug.
RW_M2E.why: Without the drug the resistant bacteria lose ground, so the drug is what keeps resistance in the population. The 'invented' option would make the drug create the gene, but the text says the gene is already carried.

RW_M2E.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “resists” most nearly mean?
RW_M2E.passage: A book sewn on cords opens flat only if the thread is drawn just tight enough to close each gathering without cinching it. A binder who pulls harder than that produces a spine that <u>resists</u> the reader, and the leaves have to be held down by hand for as long as the book is open.
RW_M2E.why: The spine is described as something the reader has to overcome by holding the leaves down, so the word names an opposing force. The 'survives damage from' sense of the word describes a material standing up to attack, which is not what the spine is doing to the reader.

RW_M2E.stem: What is the main purpose of the text?
RW_M2E.passage: A translation program trained on parallel texts learns which strings tend to appear opposite which, without being told what any of them mean. That is enough to render a weather report. It is not enough for a legal contract, where a term carries a definition fixed elsewhere in the document and a system with no notion of reference has nothing to hold on to.
RW_M2E.why: The text grants the method a success with weather reports and then names the case it cannot handle and why, which is a statement of limits. It never describes how the parallel texts are gathered.

choices.label: A
choices.content: To explain how parallel texts are collected and aligned.

choices.label: B
choices.content: To argue that legal documents should be translated only by specialists.

choices.label: C
choices.content: To compare the accuracy of two competing translation systems.

choices.label: D
choices.content: To mark the boundary of what a system trained only on parallel text can do.

RW_M2E.stem: What is the main purpose of the text?
RW_M2E.passage: Witnesses are often asked how sure they are, and juries treat the answer as a measure of how reliable the identification is. Research over four decades has found the link between the two to be strong at the moment of a first, untainted identification and weak afterwards. What happens in between is feedback: a word of encouragement, a second viewing, a remark from another witness.
RW_M2E.why: The passage separates the first untainted identification, where confidence tracks accuracy, from everything after it, and names feedback as what comes between. It stops short of recommending what juries should be told.

choices.label: A
choices.content: To describe the procedures police use when arranging an identification.

choices.label: B
choices.content: To show that most eyewitness identifications turn out to be mistaken.

choices.label: C
choices.content: To identify the conditions under which a witness's confidence does and does not track accuracy.

choices.label: D
choices.content: To argue that juries should not be told how confident a witness is.

RW_M2E.stem: According to the text, lava tubes allow a flow to travel further because they
RW_M2E.passage: A lava flow does not cool evenly. A crust forms on the surface within minutes and insulates what is beneath it, so the interior can stay fluid for weeks and go on advancing through tubes roofed by its own solidified skin. Flows that would have stopped within a few hundred metres in the open have travelled tens of kilometres in this way.
RW_M2E.why: The crust is said to insulate the interior so that it stays fluid for weeks, and that is what lets the flow keep moving. Steeper descent is never mentioned; the tube's contribution is thermal, not gravitational.

choices.label: A
choices.content: spread the flow over a wider area as it advances.

choices.label: B
choices.content: keep the interior of the flow hot enough to remain fluid.

choices.label: C
choices.content: carry the lava downhill more steeply than an open channel would.

choices.label: D
choices.content: reduce the amount of gas escaping from the lava.

RW_M2E.stem: According to the text, an invariant of the kind described can be used to
RW_M2E.passage: Knot theorists look for quantities that stay the same however a knot is pushed about. If two diagrams give different values for such a quantity, they cannot be the same knot. The reverse does not follow: two diagrams may agree on every quantity yet still be different knots, and for a long while no known quantity could separate certain pairs.
RW_M2E.why: Differing values are said to rule out sameness, while agreement is explicitly said not to establish it. Reversing the two directions gets the logic exactly backwards.

choices.label: A
choices.content: settle either question, provided enough invariants are computed.

choices.label: B
choices.content: settle neither question without an examination of the diagrams by hand.

choices.label: C
choices.content: prove that two diagrams represent different knots, but not that they represent the same knot.

choices.label: D
choices.content: prove that two diagrams represent the same knot, but not that they represent different knots.

RW_M2E.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Chaudhuri's argument?
RW_M2E.passage:
A hoist's speed governor must trip before a falling cage reaches a dangerous speed, but a governor set too finely will stop a cage that is merely descending briskly. Two settings were trialled across a year of ordinary service in a group of buildings, and the results are summarised below. Engineer Ravi Chaudhuri argues that the coarser setting gives the better balance of the two demands.
Governor settingGenuine overspeed events caughtStops on cages descending normally
Fine (0.9 m/s above rated)12 of 1247
Coarse (1.4 m/s above rated)12 of 123
RW_M2E.why: The argument needs both halves of the comparison at once: equal safety performance and far fewer nuisance stops, which is what the pairing of 12 of 12 with 3 against 47 shows. Reporting the two settings' trip speeds repeats the labels of the rows without using any of the results.

choices.label: A
choices.content: The fine setting caught 12 of 12 genuine overspeed events, which is as many as the coarse setting caught.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Both settings caught all 12 genuine overspeed events, but the coarse setting stopped only 3 normally descending cages against the fine setting's 47.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The fine setting stopped 47 normally descending cages, while the coarse setting caught 12 genuine overspeed events.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The coarse setting trips at 1.4 metres per second above the rated speed, while the fine setting trips at 0.9.

RW_M2E.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Farrow's argument?
RW_M2E.passage: Rope laid up from long fibres and rope laid up from short ones can be spun to the same diameter and the same weight. Cordage historian Ines Farrow argues that the difference between them shows itself not in a straight pull but in the way the rope holds a load that is applied and released over and over.
RW_M2E.why: Matching behaviour in a steady pull together with a divergence under repeated loading is exactly the split the argument predicts, and no other property separates the two ropes in that way. The difference in cost says nothing about how either rope behaves under load.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Long-fibre rope was more expensive to produce than short-fibre rope of the same diameter.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Short-fibre ropes absorbed more water than long-fibre ropes of the same weight.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Both kinds of rope were laid up on the same machinery at the same twist.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Ropes of the two kinds broke at nearly the same load when pulled steadily to failure, but the short-fibre ropes lost strength far faster under repeated loading and unloading.

RW_M2E.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Nwora's argument?
RW_M2E.passage: Witnesses who pick a face from a lineup are sometimes told afterwards that they chose the person the police suspected. Psychologist Adaeze Nwora argues that such a remark alters not only how confident a witness feels but also what the witness later reports about the original viewing conditions.
RW_M2E.why: A changed report of the view itself, with viewing time held constant, is the part of the claim that goes beyond confidence, and only the recollection of a longer and clearer view tests it. Greater certainty after feedback supports the confidence half alone, which the argument treats as already established.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Witnesses given confirming feedback afterwards reported feeling more certain of their choice than witnesses given no feedback.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Witnesses viewed the face for a shorter time than they later estimated.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Lineups conducted by an officer who did not know the suspect produced fewer identifications.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Witnesses given confirming feedback afterwards recalled having had a longer and clearer view of the face than witnesses given no feedback, although both groups had viewed it for the same time.

RW_M2E.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
RW_M2E.passage: A rope stored in a coil takes a set, and a rope that has taken a set runs badly through a block. Riggers therefore coil a new rope in the direction of its own lay, so that the bend the coil puts in agrees with the twist already there. A rope coiled against its lay develops kinks that no amount of pulling will take out, which means such a rope will _____
RW_M2E.why: The passage links a set to poor running through a block and then says coiling against the lay produces kinks that cannot be pulled out, so the running must suffer. Regaining the original shape is ruled out by the statement that the kinks are permanent.

choices.label: A
choices.content: run through a block less easily than one coiled with its lay.

choices.label: B
choices.content: be stronger under a straight pull than one coiled with its lay.

choices.label: C
choices.content: take a set more slowly than a rope stored uncoiled.

choices.label: D
choices.content: regain its original shape once the coil is opened.

RW_M2E.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
RW_M2E.passage: A resistance gene carried on a plasmid can pass from one bacterium to another, and often from one species to another, without either cell dividing. A gene carried on the chromosome spreads only as its owner reproduces. Where a hospital finds the same resistance gene in several unrelated species at once, the likeliest explanation is that the gene _____
RW_M2E.why: Only the plasmid is described as crossing between species without reproduction, which is what appearance in several unrelated species at once requires. Long residence on each chromosome would predict divergence between the species' copies rather than the same gene.

choices.label: A
choices.content: confers a larger advantage in some of those species than in others.

choices.label: B
choices.content: sits on a plasmid that has moved between them.

choices.label: C
choices.content: arose independently in each species under the same drug pressure.

choices.label: D
choices.content: has been carried on the chromosome of each species for a long time.

RW_M2E.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
RW_M2E.passage: Braille's six-dot cell has sixty-three usable _____ the alphabet, the digits, punctuation and a stock of contractions all fit inside that number.
RW_M2E.why: Two complete statements stand on either side of the blank and a semicolon joins them without a conjunction. A comma alone between two main clauses produces a splice.

RW_M2E.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
RW_M2E.passage: Alexander _____ who worked for decades on tabulating knots, arranged them by the smallest number of crossings in any diagram of them.
RW_M2E.why: The appositive naming his occupation is set off from the name by a comma, matching the comma that closes it before the verb. Leaving out that comma runs the name and the appositive together.

RW_M2E.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
RW_M2E.passage: The binder sews each gathering round three cords, laces the cord ends into the _____ and covers the whole in leather.
RW_M2E.why: The sentence lists three actions performed by one subject, and the last two are joined by a conjunction without a mark. Inserting a comma there would split a compound predicate.

RW_M2E.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
RW_M2E.passage: Witnesses are asked to rate their confidence immediately, before anyone has spoken to them about their _____ later ratings are worth much less.
RW_M2E.why: Both sides of the blank are complete statements, and a semicolon joins them without a conjunction. A colon followed by a conjunction is not a standard pairing.

RW_M2E.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
RW_M2E.passage: Neither the cloth grade nor the seam curves _____ enough to explain how long a sail keeps its shape.
RW_M2E.why: With a compound subject joined by the correlative pair, the verb agrees with the nearer element, which here is plural. The participle and the infinitive leave the sentence without a main verb.

RW_M2E.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
RW_M2E.passage: The yarns that go into a strand of rope _____ spun in the opposite direction to the strand itself.
RW_M2E.why: The subject is the plural noun standing before the relative clause, so the verb takes the plural form. The singular alternatives agree with the nearest noun rather than with the actual subject.

RW_M2E.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
RW_M2E.passage: A tarpaulin that is lashed down over several open crates _____ the goods beneath it from rain far better than a loose sheet does.
RW_M2E.why: The subject is the singular noun at the head of the sentence, not the plural noun inside the relative clause, so the verb is singular. The plural forms agree with the nearer noun instead of the true subject.

RW_M2E.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
RW_M2E.passage: A rope's size was long stated as the distance round it, so a three-inch line measured three inches in girth. Modern lists, _____ state the distance straight across, and the very same line is now listed at just under an inch.
RW_M2E.why: The two conventions are set against each other, one measuring round and the other across, so the transition marks a contrast. An additive marker would present the second convention as a further instance of the first.

RW_M2E.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
RW_M2E.passage: A netmaker at work measures nothing. _____ every mesh comes out the same size, because the twine is carried round a flat wooden gauge before each knot is drawn up.
RW_M2E.why: The second sentence names an outcome that stands against the absence of measuring just reported, so the transition must be contrastive. A causal marker would make the even meshes follow from measuring nothing, when what produces them is the gauge.

RW_M2E.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
RW_M2E.passage: A knot invariant that agrees on two diagrams leaves open whether the diagrams show the same knot. _____ an invariant that disagrees settles the question at once: the knots are different.
RW_M2E.why: The sentence sets the case of disagreement against the case of agreement just described, so the transition must mark opposition. A marker of similarity would claim the two cases behave alike, and the text says they do not.

RW_M2E.stem: The student wants to emphasise that neither tarred nor white cordage is better in itself. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
RW_M2E.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • Hemp cordage is sold either white or steeped in tar.
  • Tar keeps the damp out of the fibre and slows its decay.
  • Tarred cordage is stiffer and weaker for its size than white.
  • Rigging that stands out in all weathers is tarred.
  • Rope that must run freely through a block is left white.
RW_M2E.why: Showing tar winning against damp and losing on stiffness and strength, and then attaching each kind to the place that suits it, is what establishes that neither is better overall. Reporting only that tarred cordage decays more slowly makes the opposite case, naming a single winner.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Rigging that stands out in all weathers is tarred, and rope that must run freely through a block is left white.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Tar keeps the damp out of the fibre but leaves the cordage stiffer and weaker for its size, so rigging that stands out in all weathers is tarred while rope that must run freely through a block is left white.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Hemp cordage is sold either white or steeped in tar before it leaves the maker.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Tarred cordage keeps the damp out of the fibre and decays more slowly than white cordage of the same size.

RW_M2E.stem: The student wants to describe the spinning process for an audience unfamiliar with bridge building. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
RW_M2E.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • A bridge cable is spun on site from individual wires.
  • A wheel carries wires back and forth across the span.
  • The Brooklyn Bridge's cables each contain 5,434 wires.
  • The bundle is compacted and wrapped only after spinning.
  • Spinning a large cable can take several months.
RW_M2E.why: Describing the process calls for the sequence of operations, and only the sentence giving the wheel's traverse followed by compaction and wrapping supplies it. The wire count and the months taken are facts about scale rather than an account of how the work is done.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Spinning a large cable can take several months, and the bundle is compacted afterwards.

choices.label: B
choices.content: A bridge cable is spun on site rather than delivered ready made to the bridge.

choices.label: C
choices.content: A bridge cable is spun in place: a wheel carries wires back and forth across the span, and the bundle is compacted and wrapped only when all of them are laid.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The cables of the Brooklyn Bridge each contain 5,434 wires, and spinning a large cable can take several months.

RW_M2E.stem: The student wants to explain to an audience unfamiliar with the subject what each partner gains. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
RW_M2E.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • Fungal threads sheathe the roots of many forest trees.
  • The fungus receives sugar made by the tree's leaves.
  • The tree receives phosphorus the fungus draws from fine soil pores.
  • Roots cannot enter pores of that size.
  • Seedlings cut off from the network grew more slowly in one experiment.
RW_M2E.why: Both sides of the exchange have to appear, and only the sentence naming the sugar going one way and the phosphorus coming back does that. The seedling experiment shows that the network matters without saying what either partner receives.

choices.label: A
choices.content: The fungus takes sugar made by the tree's leaves and returns phosphorus drawn from soil pores too fine for any root to enter.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Fungal threads sheathe the roots of many forest trees, and seedlings cut off from the network grew more slowly in one experiment.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Roots cannot enter the fine soil pores from which the fungus draws phosphorus.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Seedlings cut off from the fungal network grew more slowly than seedlings left connected to it.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
RW_M2H.passage: The cables of a suspension bridge are not lowered into place ready made. A wheel runs back and forth across the span laying single wires, thousands of them, until the bundle is thick enough; only then is it squeezed round and bound. The finished cable is therefore _____ in place rather than delivered to it.
RW_M2H.why: The passage describes wires being laid one at a time until a cable exists where none did, which is building it on site. The 'inspected' option would describe checking a cable that already existed, which is exactly what the sentence denies.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
RW_M2H.passage: A single fibre in a rope will break at a load that varies a good deal from fibre to fibre. The rope as a whole is steadier: when one fibre parts, its share of the load is taken up by its neighbours, and the rope goes on holding. The bundle's strength is therefore more _____ than that of any strand within it.
RW_M2H.why: The contrast is between fibre strengths that vary a good deal and a rope that behaves steadily, so the blank must mean consistent from one specimen to the next. The 'impressive' option speaks to the size of the strength, not to how much it varies.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
RW_M2H.passage: Early translation programs worked from rules written out by linguists and failed on any sentence the rules had not anticipated. Later systems were given millions of sentences already translated by people and left to find the regularities themselves. The change moved the labour from stating the language to _____ the examples.
RW_M2H.why: The later systems need a large stock of existing translations, so the work becomes one of collecting them. The 'translating' option would describe producing the examples afresh, which is the very work the system is meant to take over.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
RW_M2H.passage: A ropewalk had to be as long as the rope it made, because the yarns were stretched out at full length before they were twisted together. Some ran to a quarter of a mile under one roof. The building's shape was therefore not a matter of style but a _____ of the process carried on inside it.
RW_M2H.why: The sentence contrasts style with something the process itself forced on the building, so the blank names a result of that process. The 'decoration' option would return the shape to the realm of style, which the sentence has just ruled out.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
RW_M2H.passage: A seedling growing in deep shade may draw carbon from a mature tree of another species through the fungal threads that link their roots. The transfer runs from the plant with more sugar to the plant with less. Whether the mature tree gains anything by it remains _____.
RW_M2H.why: The passage reports what is known about the direction of transfer and then marks the question of benefit as still open. The 'unpublished' option would claim the work has not appeared in print, which the text does not say.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
RW_M2H.passage: The following text is adapted from a technical history of rope manufacture. <u>Every twist in a rope is put in against the twist below it.</u> The fibres are spun one way into yarn, the yarns are turned the other way into strands, and the strands are turned back again into rope. Each layer, trying to unwind, is held by the layer it is wound against, and the rope holds itself together without any binding at all.
RW_M2H.why: The underlined sentence announces the alternating-twist rule, and the sentences after it trace that rule through fibre, yarn, strand and rope. Calling it a conclusion drawn from earlier evidence misreads its position, since nothing precedes it.

choices.label: A
choices.content: It records an objection that the rest of the text answers.

choices.label: B
choices.content: It gives an example of a practice described later in more general terms.

choices.label: C
choices.content: It draws a conclusion from evidence presented earlier in the text.

choices.label: D
choices.content: It states the principle that the rest of the text then works out in detail.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
RW_M2H.passage: The strength of a rope cannot be found by multiplying the strength of one fibre by the number of fibres in it. <u>Fibres do not all break at once.</u> The weakest give way first, and the load they were carrying passes to those still intact, which are then closer to their own limits. A rope fails in a cascade, and the total it can bear is always less than the sum of its parts.
RW_M2H.why: The first sentence says the simple multiplication fails; the underlined sentence supplies the reason, which the rest of the passage then develops into the cascade. Treating it as a counterexample to the cascade reverses the relationship, since the cascade follows from it.

choices.label: A
choices.content: It restates the opening sentence in more technical language.

choices.label: B
choices.content: It introduces the mechanism that explains the shortfall stated in the first sentence.

choices.label: C
choices.content: It qualifies a claim about fibre strength made later in the text.

choices.label: D
choices.content: It offers a counterexample to the cascade described in the final sentence.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
RW_M2H.passage: Braille is read at speed only when whole words are taken in as patterns rather than spelled out cell by cell, which is why the contracted form, with its signs for common letter groups, is taught from the start in most schools. The uncontracted form is easier to learn and slower to read, and a reader who begins with it must later unlearn the habit of tracking every letter.
RW_M2H.why: The passage weighs the contracted form's speed against the uncontracted form's ease of learning and reports that schools choose speed. Saying the uncontracted form is no longer taught overstates a text that says only that most schools begin with the other.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Contracted braille is taught first because the reading speed it allows outweighs its extra difficulty.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Uncontracted braille is no longer taught in schools.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Braille readers recognise individual cells faster than sighted readers recognise letters.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The contracted form was developed after the uncontracted form had proved too slow.

RW_M2H.stem: According to the text, what does the tree gain from the fungus?
RW_M2H.passage: The fungal threads that sheathe a tree's roots take sugar from the tree and pass back phosphorus drawn from a volume of soil the roots could never reach. Seedlings cut off from the network in one experiment grew more slowly than seedlings left connected, even where both had the same light and water. The exchange is not a favour on either side; each partner is trading a surplus for something scarce.
RW_M2H.why: The text says the threads pass back phosphorus drawn from soil the roots cannot reach. The sugar runs the other way, from tree to fungus, so naming it as the tree's gain reverses the trade.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Protection of its roots from drying out in shallow soil.

choices.label: B
choices.content: A supply of sugar that supplements what its leaves produce.

choices.label: C
choices.content: A faster rate of growth in the absence of light.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Access to phosphorus from soil beyond the reach of its own roots.

RW_M2H.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Elstad's argument?
RW_M2H.passage: A bacterial population exposed to an antibiotic can recover its numbers within days, and it is usually assumed that the survivors carry a resistance gene. Microbiologist Tomas Elstad argues that in some populations the survivors are not genetically different at all, but simply happen to be dormant when the drug arrives.
RW_M2H.why: If the survivors were genetically resistant, their descendants would survive a second dose; finding them as vulnerable as the original population is what dormancy rather than genetics predicts. Detecting resistance genes before treatment points the other way, toward the explanation the argument rejects.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Resistance genes were detected in a small fraction of the cells before treatment began.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Higher doses of the antibiotic killed a larger fraction of the population.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Survivors regrown from a treated culture were no more resistant to a second dose than the original population had been, and their descendants died at the usual rate.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The treated cultures took several days longer to recover than untreated cultures took to reach the same density.

RW_M2H.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Naess's argument?
RW_M2H.passage: Mycorrhizal fungi are often described as passing carbon between trees, but carbon moving out of one tree and into a fungus need not reach a second tree at all. Ecologist Solveig Naess argues that most of what leaves a mature tree by this route is consumed by the fungus itself.
RW_M2H.why: Following a labelled carbon atom and finding it in the fungus but not in the seedlings tests precisely where the carbon ends up. Faster growth in connected seedlings is consistent with many causes, including nutrients other than the carbon at issue.

choices.label: A
choices.content: The quantity of carbon leaving a mature tree rose when the tree was shaded.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Labelled carbon fed to a mature tree was recovered in large quantities in fungal tissue and in only trace amounts in the neighbouring seedlings connected to the same network.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Seedlings connected to a network grew faster than seedlings isolated from it.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Fungal networks were found to link trees of several different species in the same stand.

RW_M2H.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Liest's argument?
RW_M2H.passage: Charcoal from a hearth on a cave floor gives a date for the fire, not for the paintings on the wall above it. Archaeologist Gunnar Liest argues that the hearth dates commonly quoted for one decorated chamber are too early to belong to the painting of it.
RW_M2H.why: Dating the pigment directly and finding it much younger separates the fire from the painting, which is the whole of the claim. A precise date for the charcoal establishes only that the fire is well dated, leaving the link to the paintings untested.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Pigment scraped from the painted figures themselves yielded dates several thousand years later than the charcoal from the hearths below them.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The hearths contained burnt bone as well as charcoal.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Several chambers in the same cave contain hearths but no paintings.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The charcoal from the hearths was well enough preserved to give a precise date.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
RW_M2H.passage: A knot invariant is only useful if it can actually be computed for a given diagram. One classical invariant separates every pair of knots yet tabulated, but the work needed to evaluate it grows so steeply with the number of crossings that diagrams of modest size lie beyond any machine. For knots drawn with many crossings, then, this invariant is _____
RW_M2H.why: The passage grants the invariant complete success in principle and then says it cannot be evaluated for larger diagrams, which is a gap between theory and use. Saying it fails to separate knots contradicts the statement that it separates every pair tabulated.

choices.label: A
choices.content: unable to distinguish knots that other invariants can separate.

choices.label: B
choices.content: of little practical help despite its theoretical power.

choices.label: C
choices.content: the only invariant that can be relied upon.

choices.label: D
choices.content: equivalent to counting the crossings in the diagram.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
RW_M2H.passage: The tube that carries a lava flow is roofed by the flow's own crust, and the roof is thin. Where a tube runs close beneath the surface, the ground above it stands warmer than the ground on either side, and the difference persists while lava is still moving inside. A survey of surface temperatures taken from the air should therefore be able to _____
RW_M2H.why: A warm strip over an active tube that persists while lava moves is a signature visible from above, which is exactly what mapping the path requires. The passage links the warmth to the presence of moving lava but offers nothing about how much is moving.

choices.label: A
choices.content: trace the path of an active tube without the tube being opened.

choices.label: B
choices.content: measure how much lava a tube is carrying at a given moment.

choices.label: C
choices.content: predict where a new tube will form on a flow.

choices.label: D
choices.content: distinguish lava tubes from tubes that have already drained and cooled only after excavation.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
RW_M2H.passage: Wire for a bridge cable arrives on the site in coils, each _____ galvanised and tested before it leaves the mill.
RW_M2H.why: The phrase beginning with the participle modifies the coils and needs no mark to attach it. A semicolon would demand a complete statement on its right, and no verb follows.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
RW_M2H.passage: A parallel corpus is not simply two texts in two _____ every sentence in one has to be matched to the sentence that renders it in the other.
RW_M2H.why: A colon can introduce the statement that specifies what the first clause has denied. Joining the two complete statements with only a comma leaves a run-on.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
RW_M2H.passage: Because the mesh of a safety net must stretch as the load comes _____ woven from a fibre that recovers rather than one that simply resists.
RW_M2H.why: An introductory clause beginning with a subordinating conjunction is followed by a comma before the main clause. A semicolon requires a complete statement on each side, and the opening clause is not one.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
RW_M2H.passage: The sailmaker draws the seam curves full size on the loft floor, then lays the cloth over the drawing and marks _____ panels are cut only when every line has been checked.
RW_M2H.why: Two complete statements stand on either side of the blank, and a semicolon is the mark that joins them without a conjunction. A comma alone between them produces a run-on.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
RW_M2H.passage: The two diagrams look nothing alike, but they represent the same knot, and each can be deformed into _____ without cutting the strand.
RW_M2H.why: With exactly two items in view, the definite form is the one that points to the remaining member of the pair. The plural form would imply more than two diagrams.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
RW_M2H.passage: Having laid the wires one at a time across the span, the compacting machine _____ the bundle into a circular section.
RW_M2H.why: The opening participial phrase must be followed by a main clause with a finite verb. Each of the other forms leaves the sentence with no main verb at all.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
RW_M2H.passage: Because a resistance gene costs energy to maintain, bacteria carrying it grow more slowly than _____ do in the absence of the drug.
RW_M2H.why: A comparison of this kind takes a subject on the far side of the conjunction, since a verb follows the blank. The object pronoun cannot serve as the subject of that verb.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
RW_M2H.passage: New canvas draws up the first time it is wetted, and a cloth can lose most of an inch in every yard. _____ a tarpaulin cut to the exact size of the hatch it must cover will no longer reach across it after a night of rain.
RW_M2H.why: The second sentence draws the consequence of the shrinkage stated in the first, which calls for a result marker. A concessive marker would present the cover's falling short as unexpected, when it is exactly what the shrinkage predicts.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
RW_M2H.passage: Standing rigging chafes wherever it crosses a spar or another rope. _____ riggers wind the exposed length with tarred twine, laid on hard with a wooden mallet, so that the turns wear through before the rope beneath them does.
RW_M2H.why: The second sentence states what riggers do because of the chafe described in the first, so a consequence marker is called for. A concessive marker would set the two sentences against each other, as though the service were put on despite the chafe.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
RW_M2H.passage: A rope's fibres are spun one way and its strands twisted the other, so that each layer holds the layer inside it. _____ nothing binds a rope together but the tension between its own parts.
RW_M2H.why: The second sentence restates the consequence of the first in a more sweeping form, which calls for a transition marking summary. A contrast marker would suggest the two sentences disagree, and they do not.

RW_M2H.stem: The student wants to explain to an audience unfamiliar with lifts why the brake acts even when nothing else does. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
RW_M2H.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • A hoist's safety brake is worked by weights mounted on the cage.
  • The weights press outward as the cage descends.
  • Past a set speed they swing far enough to bite into the guide rails.
  • No signal from the driver or from any electrical circuit is involved.
  • Elisha Otis demonstrated an early version of such a brake in 1854.
RW_M2H.why: Acting when nothing else does is explained by the weights doing the work unaided, so the answer must join the mechanism to the absence of any signal. Naming the 1854 demonstration dates the device without saying what makes it independent.

choices.label: A
choices.content: A hoist's safety brake is worked by weights that are mounted on the cage itself.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The weights press outward as the cage descends, which is what Elisha Otis demonstrated.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Weights mounted on the cage press outward as it descends and, past a set speed, bite into the guide rails, so no signal from the driver or from any circuit is involved.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Elisha Otis demonstrated an early version of the hoist safety brake in 1854.

RW_M2H.stem: The student wants to explain to an audience unfamiliar with the subject why the soaking is not simply timed. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
RW_M2H.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • Retting soaks hemp stalks until the gum holding the fibre to the woody core has rotted.
  • The gum breaks down faster in warm water than in cold.
  • Fibre from stalks lifted too early will not part from the core.
  • Fibre from stalks left in too long crumbles when it is combed.
  • The soaking is stopped when the fibre feels ready, not after a set number of days.
RW_M2H.why: Only the sentence naming the varying rate of the rotting explains why a fixed schedule cannot serve, and the narrow window either side of it is what makes the judgement matter. Reporting that the soaking is stopped when the fibre feels ready restates the practice the student was asked to account for.

choices.label: A
choices.content: The soaking is stopped when the fibre feels ready rather than after a set number of days.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Because the gum rots faster in warm water than in cold, no set number of days suits every batch, and a batch lifted too early or left too long yields fibre that cannot be used.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Retting soaks hemp stalks until the gum holding the fibre to the woody core has rotted away.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Fibre from stalks that were left in the water too long crumbles when it is combed.

RW_M2H.stem: The student wants to explain to an audience unfamiliar with the subject why resistance can decline. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
RW_M2H.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • Making a resistance protein costs a bacterium energy.
  • Energy spent that way is not available for growth.
  • Where no drug is present, resistant strains are outgrown by others.
  • Where the drug is present, only resistant strains survive.
  • Resistance can decline in a population after a drug is withdrawn.
RW_M2H.why: The decline needs its cause attached to it, and only the sentence linking the energy cost to being outgrown after withdrawal supplies one. Restating that resistance can decline names the phenomenon without explaining it.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Where the drug is present, only resistant strains survive, and resistance can decline after it is withdrawn.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Making a resistance protein costs a bacterium energy that is not then available for growth.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Resistance can decline in a population after a drug is withdrawn from use.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Because making the protein costs energy that would otherwise go into growth, resistant strains are outgrown by others once the drug is withdrawn.

MATH_M1.stem: A ropewalk lays a warp of 720 fathoms using three grades of yarn. The number of fathoms of medium yarn is 40 more than the number of fathoms of light yarn, and the number of fathoms of heavy yarn is half the number of fathoms of light yarn. How many fathoms of heavy yarn are in the warp?
MATH_M1.check: L + (L+40) + L/2 = 720 gives 2.5L = 680, so L = 272 and the heavy yarn is 136.

MATH_M1.stem: A twine spinner is paid a fixed sum for each day worked plus a further fixed sum for each pound of twine spun beyond the daily quota. On a day when she spun 14 pounds beyond the quota she was paid $89, and on a day when she spun 22 pounds beyond the quota she was paid $113. How much is she paid, in dollars, on a day when she spins 9 pounds beyond the quota?
MATH_M1.check: $24 more for 8 more pounds is $3 a pound, so the fixed sum is 89 - 42 = 47 and 47 + 27 = 74.

MATH_M1.stem: Each bale of raw hemp yields 38 pounds of long fibre once it has been hackled. A ropewalk already holds 216 pounds of long fibre and needs at least 910 pounds in all. What is the least number of bales it must hackle?
MATH_M1.check: 910 - 216 = 694 pounds still wanted, and 694/38 is about 18.3, so 19 bales.

MATH_M1.stem: A foreman writes the equation 6(y - 4) = 2y + 44 to find the number y of yarns in one strand of a cable. A hawser is laid from 3 such strands. How many yarns are in the hawser?
MATH_M1.check: 6y - 24 = 2y + 44 gives 4y = 68 and y = 17, so three strands hold 51 yarns.

MATH_M1.stem: Tar drawn off a kettle cools at a constant rate. Its temperature was 220°F four minutes after it was drawn off and 172°F sixteen minutes after it was drawn off. According to this model, how many minutes after it was drawn off is the tar at 100°F?
MATH_M1.check: 48 degrees lost in 12 minutes is 4 a minute; 220 - 4(t-4) = 100 gives t = 34.

MATH_M1.stem: A ropewalk turns out light line at 30 fathoms an hour and heavy line at 18 fathoms an hour, and it makes only one of the two at any moment. In a 9-hour day it produced 222 fathoms of line in all. For how many hours of that day was it making heavy line?

A hand cart may carry a load of at most 512 pounds. It is already carrying 146 pounds of gear, and 40 spools weighing 0.8 pounds each are put aboard. Each coil of twine added after that weighs 3.5 pounds. What is the greatest number of coils the cart can carry?
MATH_M1.check: 512 - 146 - 32 = 334 pounds spare and 334/3.5 is about 95.4, so 95 coils.

MATH_M1.stem: For the cordage sizes used at one ropewalk, the difference \((4n+3)^{2}-(16n^{2}+5)\) gives the number of extra yarns needed to close a strand of size n. Which expression is equivalent to that difference?
MATH_M1.check: (4n+3)^2 = 16n^2 + 24n + 9, and subtracting 16n^2 + 5 leaves 24n + 4.

MATH_M1.stem: The breaking strain S, in pounds, of a tarred yarn after d days of exposure on the walk is modelled by \(S=240-\frac{d^{2}}{80}\) for \(0\le d\le 80\). After how many days does the model give a breaking strain of 195 pounds?
MATH_M1.check: d^2/80 = 45 gives d^2 = 3600, so d = 60 within the stated range.

MATH_M1.stem: A slack length of cordage is hung between two posts 8 metres apart. Its height above the floor, in centimetres, at a point x metres from the left-hand post is given by \(h(x)=2x^{2}-16x+46\) for \(0\le x\le 8\). What is the least height above the floor reached by the cordage, in centimetres?
MATH_M1.check: The vertex is at x = 4 and h(4) = 32 - 64 + 46 = 14.

MATH_M1.stem: For all \(y\ne-\frac{8}{3}\), the expression \(\frac{9y^{2}-64}{3y+8}\) is equivalent to \(3y-c\), where c is a constant. What is the value of c?
MATH_M1.check: 9y^2 - 64 = (3y+8)(3y-8), so the quotient is 3y - 8 and c = 8.

MATH_M1.stem: The function f gives the weight, in pounds, of a coil of cordage that is x fathoms long, where f(x) = 2.4x + 11. For a certain coil, f(x) = 131. What is the value of f(x + 25) for that same coil?
MATH_M1.check: Adding 25 fathoms adds 2.4(25) = 60 pounds, and 131 + 60 = 191.

MATH_M1.stem: A cordage line is stretched between two posts. Its sag y, in millimetres, at a point x metres from the left-hand post is \(y=90-(x-6)^{2}\) for \(0\le x\le 12\). What is the greatest value of x at which the sag is 65 millimetres?
MATH_M1.check: (x-6)^2 = 25 gives x = 1 or x = 11, and 11 is the greater.

MATH_M1.stem: Twine is measured out in hanks, and one hank is 840 yards. A spinner produces 7 hanks in 4 hours. Working at that same rate, how many yards of twine does the spinner produce in a 9-hour day?
MATH_M1.check: 7 hanks is 5,880 yards in 4 hours, so 1,470 yards an hour and 1,470(9) = 13,230.

MATH_M1.stem: A bale of raw hemp loses 35 percent of its weight while it is retted, and the remainder then loses a further 20 percent of its weight while it is hackled. The dressed fibre that is left weighs 195 pounds. What was the weight, in pounds, of the bale of raw hemp?
MATH_M1.check: 0.65(0.80) = 0.52 of the original remains, and 195/0.52 = 375.

MATH_M1.stem: The mean breaking load of the first 6 sample yarns cut from a run of cordage was 42 pounds. A seventh sample was then cut, and its breaking load was 70 pounds. What is the mean breaking load, in pounds, of all 7 samples?

MATH_M1.check: The ratios are 2.5, 2.6, 2.4 and 2.7, so Denhurst is greatest.

MATH_M1.stem: A foreman recorded the number of strands that broke during each of 7 runs of a ropewalk: 4, 9, 6, 4, 11, 7, and 4. What is the positive difference between the median and the mode of these 7 numbers?
MATH_M1.check: Ordered, the runs are 4, 4, 4, 6, 7, 9, 11; the median is 6, the mode is 4, and the difference is 2.

MATH_M1.stem: A hemp stack is braced by two straight stays, each of which runs from a point on a vertical post down to a stake in level ground. The first stay runs from the top of the post, 24 feet above the ground, to a stake 10 feet from the foot of the post. The second stay runs from a point 8 feet above the ground on the same post to a stake 6 feet from the foot of the post on the opposite side. What is the combined length, in feet, of the two stays?
MATH_M1.check: Two right triangles give hypotenuses of 26 and 10 feet, and 26 + 10 = 36.

MATH_M1.stem: A ropewalk's drying frame is braced by a diagonal that turns the frame into a right triangle whose legs measure 24 feet and 7 feet. What is the cosine of the angle between the 24-foot leg and the diagonal?
MATH_M1.check: The diagonal is the hypotenuse, 25 feet, and the leg adjacent to that angle is 24, so the cosine is 24/25.

MATH_M1.stem: Twine is wound onto a bobbin whose barrel is a right circular cylinder 9 centimetres long and 4 centimetres in diameter. The wound twine covers the whole length of the barrel and forms a cylindrical shell whose outer diameter is 10 centimetres. What is the volume, in cubic centimetres, of the wound twine?

A hemp-drying trestle is built as an isosceles triangle. Its apex angle measures (4x + 2)° and each of its two equal base angles measures (3x - 6)°. What is the measure, in degrees, of the apex angle?

MATH_M2E.stem: A rigger cuts a 121-foot coil of line into 8 lanyards of equal length and is left with 17 feet of line over. What is the length, in feet, of each lanyard?
MATH_M2E.check: 121 - 17 = 104 feet go into the lanyards, and 104/8 = 13.

MATH_M2E.stem: A net maker knots 26 meshes each hour. At that rate, how many meshes does the net maker knot in 7 hours?

A net maker begins with 480 meshes still to knot and knots the same number each day. The number M of meshes still to knot after d days is given by M = 480 - 32d. How many meshes does the net maker knot each day?
MATH_M2E.check: The coefficient of d is the number knotted each day, which is 32.

MATH_M2E.stem: A tarpaulin costs $7 for each square yard of canvas in it, plus a flat charge of $19 for the eyelets. One tarpaulin cost $103 in all. How many square yards of canvas are in that tarpaulin?
A sailmaker will use a needle of gauge w only if \(4w+5<33\). Which of the following values of w satisfies that condition?
MATH_M2E.check: 4w < 28 gives w < 7, and 6 is the only listed value below 7.

MATH_M2E.stem: A roll of tarpaulin holds 240 square feet of material, and each cover cut from it uses 18 square feet. After c covers have been cut, 96 square feet are left. What is the value of c?

A finished net weighs 4 pounds for each square metre of netting in it, and its frame weighs 11 pounds. The whole net must weigh no more than 96 pounds. What is the greatest whole number of square metres of netting the net can contain?
A sail loft writes the number of stitches in a panel as the product \((3m^{2})(4m^{5})\). Which expression is equivalent to that product?
MATH_M2E.check: Multiply the coefficients and add the exponents: 12 m^(2+5) = 12 m^7.

MATH_M2E.stem: A net maker writes the number of meshes in a rectangular panel as the product (x + 6)(x + 4). Which expression is equivalent to that product?
In the equation (m - 9)(m + 5) = 0, what is the positive value of m that satisfies the equation?
MATH_M2E.check: The solutions are 9 and -5, and 9 is the positive one.

MATH_M2E.stem: The function h gives the number of meshes a net maker has knotted after d days of work, where h(d) = 45d + 120. How many meshes has the net maker knotted after 6 days?

A sailmaker works a square patch of side x inches, and the function g given by \(g(x)=x^{2}+2x\) gives the number of stitches the patch takes. One patch took 63 stitches. What is the value of x for that patch?
MATH_M2E.check: x^2 + 2x = 63 gives (x+9)(x-7) = 0, and only x = 7 is a possible side length.

MATH_M2E.stem: A canvas merchant writes the cost of a bolt as 12x + 30 dollars. Which expression is equivalent to that cost?
MATH_M2E.check: 6 is the greatest common factor of 12 and 30, and 12x + 30 = 6(2x + 5).

MATH_M2E.stem: A net contains 96 meshes arranged in 8 rows, with the same number of meshes in each row. How many meshes are in each row?
A net loft holds 180 floats, and 30 percent of them are made of cork. How many of the floats are made of cork?
